PMGT1865 Week 01

PMGT1865 Week 01 - What is a Project, Project Scope and the Riverside Sounds Case

Overview

This week sets the vocabulary of project management and introduces the running case study:

• What a project is, and the four concepts used to define one: deliverable, objectives, constraints, assumptions.

• Project-management basics: the project life cycle, the ten PMBOK knowledge areas, and why planning matters.

• Project scope and scope creep.

• The Riverside Sounds case: identifying deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints and assumptions.

Key Concepts

What is a project

A project is a unique, time-limited undertaking that creates a defined product, service or result (a deliverable) in order to meet specific objectives, within constraints such as time, cost and resources. It has a defined start and end; once its objectives are met it is finished. Ongoing day-to-day operations are not projects, because they are repetitive and have no defined end.

The concepts used to define a project

• Deliverable - the verifiable product, service or result the project must produce and hand over, such as a report, a building, an event or a software system.

• Objectives - the specific outcomes the project aims to achieve; they define what success looks like.

• Constraints - the fixed limitations the project must work within, such as an immovable deadline, a set budget, or limited people and equipment.

• Assumptions - factors taken to be true for planning purposes even though they are not yet certain. If an assumption turns out to be false, the plan must be revisited, which is why assumptions are identified explicitly at the start.

Acceptance criteria

Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions a deliverable must satisfy before the sponsor or customer accepts it. They turn "the deliverable is done" into a testable statement.

Project-management basics

• Project management is the application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities in order to meet the project objectives.

• Project life cycle - the way a project's work is grouped into sequential phases from start to finish. The course uses a five-phase life cycle; whatever the phase names, phases organise the work across its life. Phases may overlap or be revisited; strict finish-before-start sequencing is not a general requirement.

• The ten PMBOK knowledge areas name the categories of concern that project management covers: integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholder management.

• Why planning matters - planning converts objectives into an executable plan: the scope is fixed, the work is scheduled, and the resources and costs are estimated. Without planning, projects drift: scope grows unnoticed, dates slip and costs rise.

Project scope and scope creep

• Project scope is all the work required to complete the project successfully - the boundary that states what is included and what is not.

• Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of scope after the plan has been set: extra features or requirements are added without a matching change to time, cost or resources. It is dangerous precisely because each addition is usually small and reasonable on its own.

Worked Examples

The Riverside Sounds case

Riverside Sounds is the running case: a festival project for its sponsor, Riverside City Council, starting Monday 17 August 2026, with a fixed festival date of Saturday 20 to Sunday 21 March 2027 and an expected audience of about 4,000 attendees.

Applying this week's concepts to the case:

Concept

How it appears in the case

Deliverable

The completed festival event and the outputs needed to stage it, to be handed over ready for the festival weekend

Acceptance criteria

The measurable conditions the council sets for accepting the result - for example, the event runs on the fixed festival dates and meets the agreed requirements

Constraints

The fixed festival date (20-21 March 2027 cannot move), the project start date, and the sponsor's budget and resource limits

Assumptions

The planning inputs taken as true - for example the expected audience of about 4,000 people, used to size the event; if actual demand differs, the plan is revisited

The distinction to carry forward: the festival date is a constraint because it is fixed and cannot be negotiated, while the expected attendance is an assumption because it is believed true for planning but is not guaranteed.
